q-274506.name: Question 1
q-274506.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=-\frac{2}{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{5}{6}.
$$

If $v$ lies in the first quadrant, then $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=${{field-1}}.
q-274506.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡v=1-{sin}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡v & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{5}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{5}^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{25}{36} \\  & =\frac{11}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{11}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})+(-\frac{2}{3})(\frac{5}{6}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}}{18}-\frac{10}{18} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{55}-10}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

q-119317.name: Question 2
q-119317.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a-b\sqrt{1}4}{6},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
q-119317.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9}-\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{9-2}{9} \\  & =\frac{7}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})+(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3})(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\  & =\frac{2}{6}-\frac{\sqrt{14}}{6} \\  & =\frac{2-1\sqrt{14}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=2,b=1,$ and $a+b=3.$

q-141359.name: Question 3
q-141359.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\frac{\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}}{4},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
q-141359.worked_solution:
First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡v=1-{cos}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡v & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{3}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the first quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{4}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}-\sqrt{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=6,b=2,$ and $a+b=8.$

q-119320.name: Question 4
q-119320.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=-\frac{2}{7},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, find the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v).$
q-119320.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{5}{9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9}-\frac{5}{9} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{4}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})+(\frac{2}{3})(-\frac{2}{7}) \\  & =-\frac{15}{21}-\frac{4}{21} \\  & =-\frac{19}{21}\end{aligned}
$$

q-119451.name: Question 5
q-119451.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=\frac{2}{7},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡v=-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7}.
$$

Given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a-b\sqrt{55}}{42},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
q-119451.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡u=1-{sin}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡u & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(\sqrt{11})^{2}}{{6}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36}{36}-\frac{11}{36} \\  & =\frac{36-11}{36} \\  & =\frac{25}{36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{25}{36}} \\  & =\pm \frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the first quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{5}{6}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{\sqrt{11}}{6})(-\frac{3\sqrt{5}}{7})+(\frac{5}{6})(\frac{2}{7}) \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{55}}{42}+\frac{10}{42} \\  & =\frac{10-3\sqrt{55}}{42}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=10,b=3,$ and $a+b=13.$

q-141389.problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=\frac{3}{4},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Given that $v$ lies in the fourth quadrant, and

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\frac{a\sqrt{3}-b\sqrt{7}}{8},
$$

calculate the value of $a+b.$
q-141389.worked_solution:
First, recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡u$, and $\operatorname{sin}⁡v.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡v+{cos}^{2}⁡v=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡v=1-{sin}^{2}⁡v
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{cos}^{2}⁡v & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡v \\  & =1-{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{4}{4}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡v & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $v$ lies in the fourth quadrant, where cosine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡v=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.
$$

We can now apply the sum formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})+(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{8}-\frac{\sqrt{7}}{8} \\  & =\frac{3\sqrt{3}-1\sqrt{7}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=3,b=1,$ and $a+b=4.$

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{sin}⁡v$, $\operatorname{cos}⁡v$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡u.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡u$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡u+{cos}^{2}⁡u=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡u=1-{cos}^{2}⁡u
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡u & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡u \\  & =1-{(-\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =1-{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{4}{9} \\  & =\frac{9}{9}-\frac{4}{9} \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡u & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{5}{9}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $u$ lies in the third quadrant, where sine is negative. So, we disregard the positive value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡u=-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(u-v) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v \\  & =(-\frac{\sqrt{5}}{3})(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})-(-\frac{2}{3})(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{6}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{2-\sqrt{15}}{6}\end{aligned}
$$
